newsitem.title: GERMANY: German output fall prompts rate cut speculation.
newsitem.headline: German output fall prompts rate cut speculation.

text.p: Another fall in German industrial output in October sent German debt prices soaring on Tuesday as market hopes of a cut in German interest rates were revived.
Industrial output fell 1.8 percent in October from the previous month, after dropping 0.6 percent in September, the economics ministry said.

The December Bund future leapt to 102.94 from 102.43 previously, and even a statement by the German Bundesbank repeating the view of its president Hans Tietmeyer that a further cut in rates was not necessary failed to halt it.
The benchmark 6.25 percent April 2006 Bund also gained to 104.73, yielding 5.578 percent, from 104.24 earlier.

Stephen King, chief European economist at James Capel in London, said the output figures, which run counter to other recent indications of a rise in German business confidence, "put the recessionary cat among the recovery pigeons".

"But this is only two months of weakness, and industrial output figures are notoriously volatile," he noted, adding that the current weakness of the mark against the dollar made an imminent German rate cut all the more unlikely.

King and others said however that the drop in output could point to weaker growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in the fourth quarter. Figures for third quarter GDP are due for release on Wednesday.
Other economists said that despite the second consecutive fall in output, there was no fundamental need for the Bundesbank to lower rates already at low levels.
"The overall environment is already positive. I think the Bundesbank has done all it can for the time being at least," said Ralf Kugelstadt, an economist at UBS in Frankfurt.
Economists contacted after the data also agreed that the central bank was unlikely to move its key rates at its next regular council meeting on Thursday.
German production had been rising gently for most of the earlier part of the year.

The latest decline includes a 2.7 percent fall in east German industrial output compared to September. Production in the west of the country fell at the slower rate of 1.7 percent compared to the month before.
The biggest drops in output during October were in the consumer durables, capital goods and manufacturing sectors, while mining was the only area were a gain was seen.

However, capital goods output showed an overall rise during September and October compared to the same two months last year, while both mining and construction output fell by more than five percent each over the same period.

In response to a Reuters query, the Bundesbank declined to comment directly on speculation about rate cuts but pointed to earlier comments by Tietmeyer that there was "no short-term reason" for an interest rate change.
